title: Yo-Yo Dieting Doesn't Wreck Your Metabolism — Healthy Habits, Not Weight Swings, Decide How Long You Live
dek: Weight cycling (yo-yo dieting) does not permanently damage metabolism, and for ordinary people the weight regained rarely means muscle loss; what actually shapes health and lifespan is the healthy habits themselves, not the up-and-down of the scale.
why: It takes the claim that "yo-yo dieting wrecks your body" and tests it along four lines — metabolism, muscle, inflammation, disease — and the conclusion is more reassuring than intuition suggests. Suited to anyone worn down by repeated failed diets.
who: People currently dieting or who have regained weight, and anyone scared off from trying again by the idea that yo-yo dieting is harmful; also for science readers who want to tell observational studies apart from randomized controlled trial evidence.
skip: You can skip the opening call-in story with John and Elena and go straight to the mechanism explanation after 12:45.

points.h: Failing at weight loss nine times is not a willpower problem
points.body: Research estimates that as many as half of American adults have experienced weight cycling at least once, and among people who weight cycle, the average is 8 times by midlife. Drummer John is on his ninth attempt at losing weight; he says he has gained and lost hundreds of pounds on and off over his life, and each regain makes him feel like he "succeeded and then failed," blaming his own self-control. But as the episode goes on to show, the hunger hormones and metabolic mechanisms in his body make it hard to keep the weight off, and they matter far more than willpower.

points.h: Your body claws the calories back below the level of awareness
points.body: Researchers gave one group of subjects a diabetes drug that makes sugar exit in urine; the subjects lost calories and lost weight, and they had no idea. As a result, the drug group felt hungry sooner and ate more than the placebo group. This happened below the level of consciousness, showing the body automatically compensates for a calorie deficit. Holding your weight is like keeping a rubber band stretched taut — slack off even slightly and it snaps back.

points.h: Slowed metabolism is an extreme case, not the general rule
points.body: The Biggest Loser study had 16 contestants lose about a third of their body weight on average, and six years later their resting metabolic rates were still about 500 calories a day below predicted — the equivalent of a Big Mac. But University of Copenhagen professor Faan points out that this group is extreme and the sample is too small. Meta-analyses show that for ordinary people metabolic suppression is on average very small, and may even fall within measurement error. So after nine cycles, John's metabolism most likely is not damaged.

points.h: There is no evidence cycling makes you fatter; the variable is age
points.body: A North Carolina study found that 74% of the weight lost was fat, but 88% of the weight regained was fat, which sounds like muscle is being lost. A German study found no such difference. The key distinction is age: the former's participants were 50-70, the latter's were 20-40. People lose muscle as they age anyway, regardless of whether they weight cycle. Almost no studies follow people through more than one full cycle, so "each cycle makes you fatter" has no evidence behind it.

points.h: Mice return to their starting weight, but the immune system remembers
points.body: Fat tissue contains large numbers of immune cells; when visceral fat cells die from lack of oxygen, macrophages come to clean them up, triggering inflammation. Alyssa Hasty put mice on a high-fat diet for 9 weeks to gain weight, then a low-fat diet to lose it, then high-fat again for 9 weeks. Compared with mice that stayed obese throughout, the cycling mice ended up with exactly the same body weight and visceral fat mass — but more T cells, and more "excitable" ones. She says the body remembers the weight swings. Still, this comes from mice on extreme diet switches, and the human evidence is murkier.

points.h: Regain it all and your diabetes risk is still lower
points.body: Observational studies show people who weight cycle have higher risks of heart failure and death, but this kind of study cannot prove causation. The answer from randomized controlled trials: even when people in a supervised weight-loss program regained all the weight, their risk of type 2 diabetes was still lower than people who never tried, and their cholesterol and blood pressure were lower too. A survey of 12,000 people found that what actually predicted mortality was healthy habits — fruits and vegetables, exercise, smoking and drinking — not BMI. So regaining the weight is not wasted effort; the healthy behavior itself is protecting you.
